demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Layla, a 31-year-old divorced Middle Eastern woman working as a social media manager, came to therapy after months of living as though her own life had become unsafe from the inside out. The event she kept returning to happened in a crowded parking lot outside a café, when she was backing her car out and struck a pedestrian she had not seen in her rear-view mirror. In the panic of hearing the impact and seeing the person crumple, she had frozen, then called for help while shaking so badly she could barely hold her phone. The injured man survived, but he required serious medical care, and Layla has never been able to experience that moment as something finished. Since then, she has been startled by unexpected touch, jerking when a coworker taps her shoulder at the office or when her ex-husband's hand brushes past her in handoff conversations, and she often reacts to ordinary moments as if danger is unfolding even when nothing is wrong. What frightened her most was not only that she had caused terrible harm, but that she no longer trusted herself to behave safely; she had come to believe she could not rely on herself to do the right thing, and that belief made the world feel filled with hidden threats. At times she looked at herself and felt unrecognisable, as if the woman she had been before the accident had been replaced by someone brittle, afraid, and permanently changed for the worse.

Her memory of the accident has remained fragmented and intensely sensory. The smell of hot asphalt, car exhaust, and the coffee she had spilled in her lap will return abruptly when she thinks about the crash, and with those smells she can feel the room narrowing around her again. Sometimes she can describe the sequence only in broken pieces, knowing what happened but being unable to find words that make the scene feel real enough to speak aloud, and in those moments she goes strangely blank, recalling the event as if it happened to a stranger. That numbness has not protected her; instead, it has deepened her fear that she is cut off from the woman who caused the injury and from any version of herself she can trust. Because she cannot fully narrate the memory, she finds herself replaying it in silence, trying to decide where she failed and whether a different person would have seen the pedestrian in time. The less she can put it into words, the more she doubts her own judgment and the more convinced she becomes that she has permanently changed for the worse.

Over the following months, those doubts and that fragmented memory kept feeding her sense that danger might appear without warning. At work in a busy digital marketing office, where colleagues often come up behind her while she is editing posts or checking campaign analytics, she stays tense in her chair and flinches at a hand on her arm, already braced for catastrophe. The smell of burnt coffee from the office kitchen or the sharp chemical scent of the parking garage can pull her back into the crash in a flash, and when that happens her body reacts before her mind catches up: her heart races, she scans for what is wrong, and she feels the same surge of fear and horror she had on the day of the accident. Those alarm reactions make her even more certain that something in her has been damaged, because she experiences them as proof that she is no longer dependable. That conviction in turn keeps the memory close and vivid, as though her mind is searching the scene again and again for the moment she should have known better, and the more she searches, the more her body stays on guard.

Layla began avoiding situations that reminded her of the accident, especially driving in crowded areas, and her world shrank around routes she thinks she can manage. She has limited her social life, partly because she is embarrassed by how easily she startles and partly because she does not want anyone to see how much guilt and shame she carries. At times she wonders if her divorce was hastened by the way she withdrew, becoming watchful and self-protective, unable to explain why a casual touch or a familiar street could leave her overwhelmed. She finally sought help after another near-miss in the office parking lot, when a coworker reached around her car to close the door and she jerked away with such panic that she had to sit in the driver's seat until she stopped shaking. What brought her in was the fear that this narrow, frightened version of herself will become permanent, and what she most hopes for is to trust her own mind and body again without feeling that the accident is still happening every time someone comes too close.
